This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** prediction-problems-risks-and-empirical-minimization / prediction-problems-risks-and-empirical-minimization-examples. **Scope:** Define measurable instance and label spaces with product sigma-algebra, joint law $P$, measurable predictor class, nonnegative measurable loss, population risk $R_P(f)=E_P[\\ell(f(X),Y)]$ as an extended nonnegative integral, empirical risk $R_m(f)=m^{-1}\\sum_{i=1}^m\\ell(f(X_i),Y_i)$, class Bayes risk $R_P^*(\\mathcal F)=\\inf_{f\\in\\mathcal F}R_P(f)$ and unrestricted Bayes risk $R_P^*=\\inf_fR_P(f)$ over measurable predictors, excess risk $R_P(f)-R_P^*(\\mathcal F)$ when finite, and exact versus approximate ERM. Define excess-risk differences only when risks being subtracted are finite. A conditional Bayes rule requires a regular conditional label law (for example, standard-Borel label target) and an attained measurable pointwise minimizer; do not infer conditional laws on arbitrary measurable spaces. The published standard-Borel conditional-law existence theorem and the published L2 conditional-projection theorem each assume AC, so state/carry AC when those interfaces are used; the finite-label conditional-expectation route may be stated directly. Proposed interfaces: `def-supervised-learning-problem`, `def-population-and-empirical-risk`, `def-bayes-predictor-and-excess-risk`, `def-empirical-risk-minimizer`, `alg-finite-list-empirical-risk-minimizer`, `alg-approximate-erm`. The finite-list algorithm takes the observed sample and an ordered finite nonempty list of measurable predictors and finite tolerance $\\eta\\ge0$, evaluates every empirical risk in $[0,+\\infty]$, and returns the first minimizer if all empirical risks are $+\\infty$; otherwise it returns the first predictor with finite empirical risk at most the finite list minimum plus $\\eta$. This defines exact ERM when $\\eta=0$, avoids the undefined expression $+\\infty+\\eta$, and is measurable by finite comparisons of extended-real measurable functions. An infinite class requires a separately stated measurable-selector premise, not a generic executable procedure. Distinguish training risk, population risk, prediction error, and parameter error. **Proof route:** measurability and integration for risk definitions; pointwise conditional minimization only under the conditional-law and selector premises; no existence theorem without compactness/continuity or stated attainment/selection. **Examples:** binary 0–1 loss, squared loss conditional mean, absolute loss conditional median, nonattained infimum. **Requires:** `probability-spaces-random-variables-and-expectation` (`def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element`, `def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable`, `thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets`, `thm-conditional-expectation-is-the-l2-orthogonal-projection` when used, with their AC premises); earlier MSF-01 — Statistical Experiments, Models and Identifiability (`def-statistical-experiment`, `def-parametric-statistical-model`); MSF-03 — Loss, Risk and Decision Theory (`def-loss-function-and-risk`, `thm-bayes-rule-minimizes-prior-risk`). **Sources:** Mohri, Rostamizadeh, and Talwalkar, *Foundations of Machine Learning*, 2e, Chapter 2 §§2.1–2.4, Theorems 2.5 and 2.13 with complete proofs, physical PDF pp. 26–45; §2.4 for iid supervised setup. The realizable proof is the bad-consistent-hypothesis event and $(1-\\epsilon)^m\\le e^{-m\\epsilon}$; the agnostic result is Hoeffding plus a finite-class union bound. This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** finite-class-pac-learning-and-erm / finite-class-pac-learning-and-erm-examples. **Scope:** For binary classifiers with zero-one risk, for $0<\\epsilon,\\delta<1$, call $A$ $(\\epsilon,\\delta)$-PAC realizable if for every iid law with a target $h^*\\in H$ of zero risk, $P_S[R(A(S))\\le\\epsilon]\\ge1-\\delta$; call it agnostic $(\\epsilon,\\delta)$-PAC if for every iid law $P$, $P_S[R(A(S))-\\inf_{h\\in H}R(h)\\le\\epsilon]\\ge1-\\delta$. Using the choice-free published `thm-finite-class-uniform-deviation`, for finite nonempty $H$, iid observations, and losses in $[0,1]$, state the two-sided uniform deviation $|R(h)-\\widehat R(h)|\\le\\sqrt{(\\log|H|+\\log(2/\\delta))/(2m)}$ simultaneously for all $h$ with probability at least $1-\\delta$. In the realizable binary case, if the target lies in $H$ and the learner returns a consistent member, then error is at most $\\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\\delta$ whenever $m\\ge(\\log|H|+\\log(1/\\delta))/\\epsilon$. Keep the realizable and noisy/agnostic rates distinct. State measurability and existence, or use an infimum and measurable approximate selector; the finite-list algorithm in ML-01 gives an operational selector. This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** rademacher-complexity-and-generalization / rademacher-complexity-and-generalization-examples. **Scope:** Use Mohri et al.'s normalization throughout: for $S=(z_1,\\ldots,z_m)$ and loss class $G\\subseteq[0,1]^Z$, define $\\widehat{\\mathfrak R}_S(G)=E_\\sigma[\\sup_{g\\in G}m^{-1}\\sum_i\\sigma_i g(z_i)]$ for independent uniform signs $\\sigma_i\\in\\{-1,+1\\}$ and $\\mathfrak R_m(G)=E_{S\\sim P^m}\\widehat{\\mathfrak R}_S(G)$. Assume the suprema are measurable or state outer probability. Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) for the following concentration-based generalization and ERM bounds, as required by the reused McDiarmid supplier. With probability at least $1-\\delta$, simultaneously for all $g\\in G$, give the one-sided bounds $Pg\\le P_mg+2\\mathfrak R_m(G)+\\sqrt{\\log(1/\\delta)/(2m)}$ and $Pg\\le P_mg+2\\widehat{\\mathfrak R}_S(G)+3\\sqrt{\\log(2/\\delta)/(2m)}$. Use $\\widehat{\\mathfrak R}_S(1-G)=\\widehat{\\mathfrak R}_S(G)$, apply the same bounds to $1-G$, and take a union bound for two-sided deviation: with probability $1-\\delta$, $\\sup_g|Pg-P_mg|\\le2\\mathfrak R_m(G)+\\sqrt{\\log(2/\\delta)/(2m)}$, or empirically $2\\widehat{\\mathfrak R}_S(G)+3\\sqrt{\\log(4/\\delta)/(2m)}$. Hence an $\\eta$-approximate ERM in this same class has excess at most $4\\mathfrak R_m(G)+2\\sqrt{\\log(2/\\delta)/(2m)}+\\eta$, or empirically $4\\widehat{\\mathfrak R}_S(G)+6\\sqrt{\\log(4/\\delta)/(2m)}+\\eta$. For scalar coordinate maps $\\Phi_i$ that are $L$-Lipschitz, state Mohri Lemma 5.7 in this nonabsolute convention: $E_\\sigma\\sup_{h\\in H}\\sum_i\\sigma_i\\Phi_i(h(z_i))\\le L E_\\sigma\\sup_{h\\in H}\\sum_i\\sigma_i h(z_i)$, for a finite/countable or separably measurable class with finite measurable suprema. No zero-at-zero assumption is needed because the fixed coordinate offsets cancel under the signs. Keep the separate two-sided absolute-sup contraction factor $2L$ distinct; never mix Bartlett–Mendelson's alternate normalization. Proposed interfaces: `def-rademacher-complexity`, `thm-rademacher-symmetrization-bound`, `thm-rademacher-contraction-inequality`, `thm-rademacher-uniform-generalization`, `cor-erm-excess-risk-from-uniform-deviation`. **Proof route:** independent ghost sample, Jensen, Rademacher sign symmetrization, bounded-difference tail; for lower deviation apply the theorem to complemented losses, then use the ERM comparison. **Examples:** finite class, linear predictors on a bounded ball, and a loose bound whose radius dependence is visible. **Requires:** ML-01; ML-02; MSF-19 — Empirical-Process Complexity (`def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process`, `thm-independent-process-symmetrization`, `thm-rademacher-contraction`, `thm-finite-class-uniform-deviation`); MSF-18 — Concentration (`thm-mcdiarmid-bounded-differences`). **Sources:** Mohri et al., *Foundations of Machine Learning*, 2e, Definition 3.1, Theorem 3.3 and proof, physical PDF pp. 30–33, for the declared normalization and constants; Bartlett and Mendelson, “Rademacher and Gaussian Complexities: Risk Bounds and Structural Results,” JMLR 3 (2002), Theorems 5, 7–9, 12 and Appendices A–B for comparison. This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** algorithmic-stability-and-generalization / algorithmic-stability-and-generalization-examples. **Scope:** Use Bousquet–Elisseeff's deletion convention: a permutation-invariant algorithm $A$ has uniform stability $\\beta_m$ if $\\sup_{S\\in\\mathcal Z^m,\\,1\\le i\\le m,\\,z\\in\\mathcal Z}|\\ell(A_S,z)-\\ell(A_{S\\setminus i},z)|\\le\\beta_m$, where $S\\setminus i$ deletes the indexed observation $i$ and the sequence $\\beta_m$ is nonincreasing in $m$. Define $R_{\\rm loo}(A,S)=m^{-1}\\sum_{i=1}^m\\ell(A_{S\\setminus i},Z_i)$. This is not replace-one stability; deletion stability implies a replace-one loss change at most $2\\beta_m$. For iid $S$ with bounded losses, the expected gap obeys $E_S[R(A_S)-\\widehat R_S(A_S)]\\le2\\beta_m$. Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) for the following high-probability bounds, as required by the reused McDiarmid supplier. If $0\\le\\ell(A_S,z)\\le M$ for every $S,z$, then for each $\\delta\\in(0,1)$ the separate high-probability bounds are $R(A_S)\\le\\widehat R_S(A_S)+2\\beta_m+(4m\\beta_m+M)\\sqrt{\\log(1/\\delta)/(2m)}$ and $R(A_S)\\le R_{\\rm loo}(A_S)+\\beta_m+(4m\\beta_m+M)\\sqrt{\\log(1/\\delta)/(2m)}$, each with probability at least $1-\\delta$. For fixed $\\lambda>0$, define the RKHS regularized ERM as the attained minimizer of $m^{-1}\\sum_i\\ell(f,z_i)+\\lambda\\|f\\|_{\\mathcal H}^2$; if $K(x,x)\\le\\kappa^2$ and $\\ell$ is convex and $\\sigma$-admissible, meaning $|\\ell(f,(x,y))-\\ell(g,(x,y))|\\le\\sigma|f(x)-g(x)|$, then $\\beta_m\\le\\sigma^2\\kappa^2/(2\\lambda m)$. This condition does not itself establish the separate bounded-loss premise. Proposed interfaces: `def-uniform-algorithmic-stability`, `thm-uniform-stability-expected-generalization`, `thm-uniform-stability-high-probability-generalization`, `thm-strongly-convex-regularized-erm-stability`. **Proof route:** the expected-gap identity replaces a deleted training example by an independent test point; bound the loss change by $\\beta_m$ or $2\\beta_m$ according to the identity used. For the tail bound, compare delete-one changes of $R$ and empirical risk, then apply bounded differences with coordinate oscillation $4\\beta_m+M/m$. **Examples:** strongly convex regularized loss, unstable nearest-neighbor classifier, stability versus training accuracy. **Requires:** ML-01 risk and iid notation; ML-04 only for comparison; MSF-18 — Concentration (`thm-mcdiarmid-bounded-differences`). **Sources:** Bousquet and Elisseeff, “Stability and Generalization,” JMLR 2 (2002), full paper and Appendix proofs, Definitions 6 and 8, Lemma 7, Theorem 12 (printed pp. 504–508), Theorem 22 and Lemma 23 (pp. 514–516). Use this deletion convention and its constants consistently; optimization convergence alone does not imply stability.",

This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** compression-and-pac-bayes-generalization / compression-and-pac-bayes-generalization-examples. **Scope:** Define a deterministic compression map that selects at most $d$ labeled sample entries and a fixed reconstruction map returning any binary hypothesis (not necessarily in $H$); a consistent compression learner must reproduce all sample labels. For a fixed target concept $c\\in H$, domain law $D$, iid labeled sample $Z_i=(X_i,c(X_i))$ with $X_i\\sim D$, integer $m>d$, $\\epsilon\\in(0,1)$, and no extra side information, state $\\Pr_{D^m}\\{\\text{some index subset }I\\subseteq[m], |I|\\le d,\\text{ has }R_D(g(Z_I))>\\epsilon\\text{ while }g(Z_I)\\text{ is consistent on the full sample}\\}\\le\\sum_{i=0}^d\\binom mi(1-\\epsilon)^{m-i}$. ## Exact spaces, hypotheses and interfaces

Fix d>=1, T>0, 0<epsilon<T. Let mu be a Borel probability on R^d supported in the closed ball of finite radius R. Let g:[0,T]->(0,infinity) be C1 and satisfy 0<g_min<=g(t)<=g_max<infinity; put v(t)=integral_0^t g(r)^2 dr. Assume AC exactly as in the published Itô strong-solution and conditional-expectation suppliers. On their usual complete filtered probability space take X0 with law mu independent of the d-dimensional Brownian future. Set X_t=X0+integral_0^t g(r)dW_r. Existing global Lipschitz/linear-growth SDE existence and finite moments are reusable; no new generic SDE existence result is proposed. mu need not have a Lebesgue density, can be singular/discrete and need not be Gaussian. The reverse initial law X_T is unbounded in general.

Proposed local prerequisite items, in this order:

1. `lem-deterministic-ito-integral-has-gaussian-independent-increments`: the integral over [s,t] has independent centered Gaussian law with covariance [v(t)−v(s)]I, independent of the past. Start with step integrands; independent Brownian Gaussian increments give their joint characteristic function. Approximate deterministic continuous g in L2 by step integrands. Itô isometry gives L2 convergence; |exp(iu·z)−exp(iu·w)|<=|u||z−w| gives characteristic-function convergence. The same joint calculation with an arbitrary bounded past measurable variable preserves independence. Uniqueness of finite characteristic functions identifies the Gaussian law; if the library characteristic-function uniqueness theorem cannot be used with its exact finite-law hypotheses, prove this finite Gaussian-convolution specialization locally via Fourier inversion for the smooth Gaussian density. No martingale representation theorem is needed.
2. `def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density`: let phi_v(z)=(2 pi v)^(−d/2)exp(−|z|^2/(2v)); for t>0 define p_t(x)=integral phi_v(t)(x−z) mu(dz), and q(s,x;t,y)=phi_(v(t)−v(s))(y−x). Positive Gaussian integration gives a strictly positive normalized density by Tonelli and the published multivariate-normal density/change-of-variables construction. Its transition law follows from item 1; finite Gaussian covariance addition gives Chapman–Kolmogorov. This definition discharges density existence for this branch, with no assumption that mu itself has a density.
3. `thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation`: on every [epsilon,T], p is C1 in time and C-infinity in space and solves partial_t p=(g(t)^2/2) Delta p. For any finite derivative order, the derivative of phi_v is a polynomial times the same Gaussian; with v bounded below and z in a fixed compact ball, its absolute value on each compact x-neighborhood has a uniform integrable constant. Differentiation under the finite measure integral is therefore justified by dominated convergence. The same calculation differentiates the explicit kernel; integrating its Laplacian gives zero by Gaussian tails. On R^d, uniqueness among probability-law-valued weak forward solutions with narrowly continuous t and prescribed initial law follows by testing against the bounded smooth backward solution h(s,x)=integral phi_(v(t)−v(s))(y−x)f(y)dy for f smooth compactly supported. Cut off h spatially, let the cutoff radius increase using bounded derivatives and finite total mass, then obtain integral f dmu_t=integral h(0,x)mu(dx). Thus the explicit heat semigroup identifies the law; no unspecified boundary condition or uniqueness theorem is invoked. Endpoint h(t)=f is obtained by dominated convergence/Gaussian approximate identity.

**Requires:** existing P-SDE-01 strong SDE/moment interface; published Brownian/Itô isometry, multivariate Gaussian density and finite characteristic-function uniqueness, Tonelli/dominated convergence and probability-law/weak-convergence interfaces. Exact item-level edges and local alternatives are enumerated in the normative module. No machine-learning result is a supplier. **Examples:** point-mass/finite-mixture initial law; a compactly supported singular law whose positive-time density is smooth; score bounds deteriorating as epsilon decreases; a Gaussian increment coupling giving the endpoint W2 bound. The B page is a leaf and is never a logical prerequisite. **Sources:** explicit Gaussian-convolution/Itô argument in the normative module plus its published local suppliers; inherited Anderson/Song references are context, not a claimed rereading or a substitute for these proofs.

## Incorporated complete prerequisite module

# Constructive density and reversal prerequisite closure

This addendum is part of the new probability pair P-SDE-03 and existing machine-learning pair P-SDE-02, preserving P-SDE-01 and all original stable IDs/conditional Anderson contracts. Items 1–4 and 8 belong to the new P-SDE-03 A page; items 5–7 belong to P-SDE-02. The published P-SDE-01 is reused without extension. It supplies an unconditional, nontrivial learning regime without an unspecified parabolic density theorem. It is a complete local prerequisite design and argument, not an authored/accepted proof. The broad conditional theorem does not supply any density assertion unless its full stated hypotheses have been established; the following module is the concrete branch available to ML-60 without that import.

## Exact spaces, hypotheses and interfaces

Fix d>=1, T>0, 0<epsilon<T. Let mu be a Borel probability on R^d supported in the closed ball of finite radius R. Let g:[0,T]->(0,infinity) be C1 and satisfy 0<g_min<=g(t)<=g_max<infinity; put v(t)=integral_0^t g(r)^2 dr. Assume AC exactly as in the published Itô strong-solution and conditional-expectation suppliers. On their usual complete filtered probability space take X0 with law mu independent of the d-dimensional Brownian future. Set X_t=X0+integral_0^t g(r)dW_r. Existing global Lipschitz/linear-growth SDE existence and finite moments are reusable; no new generic SDE existence result is proposed. mu need not have a Lebesgue density, can be singular/discrete and need not be Gaussian. The reverse initial law X_T is unbounded in general.

Proposed local prerequisite items, in this order:

1. `lem-deterministic-ito-integral-has-gaussian-independent-increments`: the integral over [s,t] has independent centered Gaussian law with covariance [v(t)−v(s)]I, independent of the past. Start with step integrands; independent Brownian Gaussian increments give their joint characteristic function. Approximate deterministic continuous g in L2 by step integrands. Itô isometry gives L2 convergence; |exp(iu·z)−exp(iu·w)|<=|u||z−w| gives characteristic-function convergence. The same joint calculation with an arbitrary bounded past measurable variable preserves independence. Uniqueness of finite characteristic functions identifies the Gaussian law; if the library characteristic-function uniqueness theorem cannot be used with its exact finite-law hypotheses, prove this finite Gaussian-convolution specialization locally via Fourier inversion for the smooth Gaussian density. No martingale representation theorem is needed.
2. `def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density`: let phi_v(z)=(2 pi v)^(−d/2)exp(−|z|^2/(2v)); for t>0 define p_t(x)=integral phi_v(t)(x−z) mu(dz), and q(s,x;t,y)=phi_(v(t)−v(s))(y−x). Positive Gaussian integration gives a strictly positive normalized density by Tonelli and the published multivariate-normal density/change-of-variables construction. Its transition law follows from item 1; finite Gaussian covariance addition gives Chapman–Kolmogorov. This definition discharges density existence for this branch, with no assumption that mu itself has a density.
3. `thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation`: on every [epsilon,T], p is C1 in time and C-infinity in space and solves partial_t p=(g(t)^2/2) Delta p. For any finite derivative order, the derivative of phi_v is a polynomial times the same Gaussian; with v bounded below and z in a fixed compact ball, its absolute value on each compact x-neighborhood has a uniform integrable constant. Differentiation under the finite measure integral is therefore justified by dominated convergence. The same calculation differentiates the explicit kernel; integrating its Laplacian gives zero by Gaussian tails. On R^d, uniqueness among probability-law-valued weak forward solutions with narrowly continuous t and prescribed initial law follows by testing against the bounded smooth backward solution h(s,x)=integral phi_(v(t)−v(s))(y−x)f(y)dy for f smooth compactly supported. Cut off h spatially, let the cutoff radius increase using bounded derivatives and finite total mass, then obtain integral f dmu_t=integral h(0,x)mu(dx). Thus the explicit heat semigroup identifies the law; no unspecified boundary condition or uniqueness theorem is invoked. Endpoint h(t)=f is obtained by dominated convergence/Gaussian approximate identity.
4. `thm-gaussian-mixture-score-and-global-lipschitz-bound`: define the posterior weighting nu_(t,x)(dz)=phi_v(t)(x−z)mu(dz)/p_t(x). It is a probability kernel by positive p and measurability. Direct differentiation gives score_t(x)=−[x−m_(t,x)]/v(t), m_(t,x)=integral z nu_(t,x)(dz), and D_x score=−I/v(t)+Cov_nu(Z)/v(t)^2. Since |Z|<=R, ||Cov_nu(Z)||<=R^2. Hence uniformly on [epsilon,T], ||D score||<=1/v(epsilon)+R^2/v(epsilon)^2, and |score_t(x)|<=(|x|+R)/v(epsilon). The bound follows from u^T Cov u<=E(u·Z)^2<=R^2|u|^2. This is a verified global state-Lipschitz/linear-growth contract; it is not asserted for arbitrary unbounded data measures.
5. `def-bayes-reversed-gaussian-smoothing-kernels`: for 0<=u<w<=T−epsilon, define K_(u,w)(y,dx)=p_(T−w)(x)q(T−w,x;T−u,y)dx/p_(T−u)(y), and Y0 law p_T. The forward marginal identity normalizes this probability kernel at every y. Multiplication cancels the intermediate p and forward Chapman–Kolmogorov proves reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov. Iterated Bayes proves its finite-dimensional laws coincide with (X_(T−u)); no abstract infinite product construction is necessary, because the forward process already has continuous paths.
6. `lem-reversed-smoothing-generator-and-martingale`: for compactly supported smooth phi and t=T−u, write the small-time reversed conditional expectation as [P^*_(t−h,t)(p_(t−h)phi)](y)/p_t(y). Differentiate the explicit Gaussian kernel, use the preceding forward equation, and Taylor-expand at h=0 to obtain the generator [L_t^*(p_t phi)−phi L_t^*p_t]/p_t=(g(t)^2/2)Delta phi+g(t)^2 score_t·grad phi. The sign is plus score; the drift of the original pure-noise process is zero. To justify this on compact y neighborhoods, p_t has a strictly positive compact minimum and every differentiated Gaussian convolution is locally uniformly bounded on [epsilon,T]; tails have Gaussian decay since mu is compact. Finite difference quotients thus converge locally uniformly. Differentiate K_(u,w)phi under the integral (or integrate the same generator identity) to get K_(u,w)phi−phi=integral_u^w K_(u,r) Ltilde_r phi dr. Conditioning at successive times gives phi(Y_w)−phi(Y_u)−integral_u^w Ltilde_r phi(Y_r)dr as a martingale increment after localization to a bounded ball. This supplies the generator-to-martingale step rather than assuming a separate reverse martingale-problem theorem.
7. `thm-gaussian-smoothing-reversal-on-truncated-time-interval`: localize the coordinate functions x_i and products x_i x_j by smooth cutoffs and use item 6. The continuous local martingale M_u=Y_u−Y0−integral_0^u g(T−r)^2 score_(T−r)(Y_r)dr has brackets [M_i,M_j]_u=delta_ij integral_0^u g(T−r)^2dr. Define B_u=integral_0^u g(T−r)^(−1)dM_r by localized L2 integration; inverse g is bounded. Its brackets are delta_ij u. Prove the required Lévy characterization locally: complex Itô applied to exp(i theta·(B_t−B_s)+|theta|^2(t−s)/2) yields a local martingale whose modulus is bounded by exp(|theta|^2T/2), hence is a true martingale after stopped dominated convergence. Therefore E[exp(i theta·(B_t−B_s))|F_s]=exp(−|theta|^2(t−s)/2); finite characteristic-function uniqueness gives Gaussian increments independent of the reverse past. Thus B is Brownian in the reversed filtration and dY_u=g(T−u)^2 score_(T−u)(Y_u)du+g(T−u)dB_u. Item 4 verifies the global state-Lipschitz/linear-growth drift premise of the published strong existence/pathwise uniqueness theorem on [0,T−epsilon]. The time dependence is Borel/continuous, and Y0 has finite second moment and is independent of future B increments by the same conditional characteristic-function statement. This identifies the unique law of the reversed SDE without imposing Anderson's bounded reverse initial law or an unspecified augmented KFP theorem.
8. `thm-gaussian-smoothing-endpoint-weak-limit`: E|X_epsilon−X0|^2=d v(epsilon)->0. Hence X_epsilon converges in probability and weakly to mu; coupling gives W2 distance at most sqrt(d v(epsilon)). The exact reversed endpoint law at time T−epsilon consequently approaches mu. No regular score, Lipschitz drift, or solver-uniform error constant is asserted at the singular endpoint epsilon=0. Total generative error must separately bound endpoint truncation, learned-score error and numerical discretization; letting step size decrease does not remove either of the first two.

## Dependency closure and breadth boundary

The module needs only published finite Gaussian laws/densities, finite independent products, Tonelli/dominated convergence, characteristic functions/uniqueness or the explicit finite Gaussian-convolution proof above, scalar Itô isometry and formula coordinatewise, continuous local martingales and quadratic covariation (with stopped stochastic integration supplied in item 7 if unavailable), and published global strong Lipschitz SDE well-posedness/moments. Its new local obligations are explicitly enumerated in items 1–8; none calls the broad density theorem or assumes its own reversal conclusion. Measurable posterior kernels are explicit density ratios, so no additional measurable-selection theorem is hidden.

This gives a complete proof design for the additive Gaussian-smoothing branch of ML-60 and actual initial-law weak-limit closure. P-SDE-02's original general state-dependent theorem is retained as a conditional result with its full density/semigroup hypotheses, not applied to every neural drift or nonlinear forward diffusion. For an unconditional theorem for arbitrary smooth uniformly elliptic state-dependent coefficients, a separate parametrix/heat-kernel module is still required; its absence does not justify claiming such a theorem here. Likewise the untouched Wasserstein-gradient-flow and random-matrix prerequisite designs retain their original explicit local obligations; no source reading or proof completion for them is fabricated by this addition.

## Exact spaces, hypotheses and interfaces

Fix d>=1, T>0, 0<epsilon<T. Let mu be a Borel probability on R^d supported in the closed ball of finite radius R. Let g:[0,T]->(0,infinity) be C1 and satisfy 0<g_min<=g(t)<=g_max<infinity; put v(t)=integral_0^t g(r)^2 dr. Assume AC exactly as in the published Itô strong-solution and conditional-expectation suppliers. On their usual complete filtered probability space take X0 with law mu independent of the d-dimensional Brownian future. Set X_t=X0+integral_0^t g(r)dW_r. Existing global Lipschitz/linear-growth SDE existence and finite moments are reusable; no new generic SDE existence result is proposed. mu need not have a Lebesgue density, can be singular/discrete and need not be Gaussian. The reverse initial law X_T is unbounded in general.

Proposed local prerequisite items, in this order:

1. `lem-deterministic-ito-integral-has-gaussian-independent-increments`: the integral over [s,t] has independent centered Gaussian law with covariance [v(t)−v(s)]I, independent of the past. Start with step integrands; independent Brownian Gaussian increments give their joint characteristic function. Approximate deterministic continuous g in L2 by step integrands. Itô isometry gives L2 convergence; |exp(iu·z)−exp(iu·w)|<=|u||z−w| gives characteristic-function convergence. The same joint calculation with an arbitrary bounded past measurable variable preserves independence. Uniqueness of finite characteristic functions identifies the Gaussian law; if the library characteristic-function uniqueness theorem cannot be used with its exact finite-law hypotheses, prove this finite Gaussian-convolution specialization locally via Fourier inversion for the smooth Gaussian density. No martingale representation theorem is needed.
2. `def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density`: let phi_v(z)=(2 pi v)^(−d/2)exp(−|z|^2/(2v)); for t>0 define p_t(x)=integral phi_v(t)(x−z) mu(dz), and q(s,x;t,y)=phi_(v(t)−v(s))(y−x). Positive Gaussian integration gives a strictly positive normalized density by Tonelli and the published multivariate-normal density/change-of-variables construction. Its transition law follows from item 1; finite Gaussian covariance addition gives Chapman–Kolmogorov. This definition discharges density existence for this branch, with no assumption that mu itself has a density.
3. `thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation`: on every [epsilon,T], p is C1 in time and C-infinity in space and solves partial_t p=(g(t)^2/2) Delta p. For any finite derivative order, the derivative of phi_v is a polynomial times the same Gaussian; with v bounded below and z in a fixed compact ball, its absolute value on each compact x-neighborhood has a uniform integrable constant. Differentiation under the finite measure integral is therefore justified by dominated convergence. The same calculation differentiates the explicit kernel; integrating its Laplacian gives zero by Gaussian tails. On R^d, uniqueness among probability-law-valued weak forward solutions with narrowly continuous t and prescribed initial law follows by testing against the bounded smooth backward solution h(s,x)=integral phi_(v(t)−v(s))(y−x)f(y)dy for f smooth compactly supported. Cut off h spatially, let the cutoff radius increase using bounded derivatives and finite total mass, then obtain integral f dmu_t=integral h(0,x)mu(dx). Thus the explicit heat semigroup identifies the law; no unspecified boundary condition or uniqueness theorem is invoked. Endpoint h(t)=f is obtained by dominated convergence/Gaussian approximate identity.
4. `thm-gaussian-mixture-score-and-global-lipschitz-bound`: define the posterior weighting nu_(t,x)(dz)=phi_v(t)(x−z)mu(dz)/p_t(x). It is a probability kernel by positive p and measurability. 5. `def-bayes-reversed-gaussian-smoothing-kernels`: for 0<=u<w<=T−epsilon, define K_(u,w)(y,dx)=p_(T−w)(x)q(T−w,x;T−u,y)dx/p_(T−u)(y), and Y0 law p_T. To justify this on compact y neighborhoods, p_t has a strictly positive compact minimum and every differentiated Gaussian convolution is locally uniformly bounded on [epsilon,T]; tails have Gaussian decay since mu is compact. Finite difference quotients thus converge locally uniformly. Differentiate K_(u,w)phi under the integral (or integrate the same generator identity) to get K_(u,w)phi−phi=integral_u^w K_(u,r) Ltilde_r phi dr. The module needs only published finite Gaussian laws/densities, finite independent products, Tonelli/dominated convergence, characteristic functions/uniqueness or the explicit finite Gaussian-convolution proof above, scalar Itô isometry and formula coordinatewise, continuous local martingales and quadratic covariation (with stopped stochastic integration supplied in item 7 if unavailable), and published global strong Lipschitz SDE well-posedness/moments. # Constructive density and reversal prerequisite closure

This addendum is part of the new probability pair P-SDE-03 and existing machine-learning pair P-SDE-02, preserving P-SDE-01 and all original stable IDs/conditional Anderson contracts. Items 1–4 and 8 belong to the new P-SDE-03 A page; items 5–7 belong to P-SDE-02. The published P-SDE-01 is reused without extension. ## Exact spaces, hypotheses and interfaces

Fix d>=1, T>0, 0<epsilon<T. Let mu be a Borel probability on R^d supported in the closed ball of finite radius R. Let g:[0,T]->(0,infinity) be C1 and satisfy 0<g_min<=g(t)<=g_max<infinity; put v(t)=integral_0^t g(r)^2 dr. Assume AC exactly as in the published Itô strong-solution and conditional-expectation suppliers. On their usual complete filtered probability space take X0 with law mu independent of the d-dimensional Brownian future. Set X_t=X0+integral_0^t g(r)dW_r. Existing global Lipschitz/linear-growth SDE existence and finite moments are reusable; no new generic SDE existence result is proposed. mu need not have a Lebesgue density, can be singular/discrete and need not be Gaussian. The reverse initial law X_T is unbounded in general.

Proposed local prerequisite items, in this order:

1. `lem-deterministic-ito-integral-has-gaussian-independent-increments`: the integral over [s,t] has independent centered Gaussian law with covariance [v(t)−v(s)]I, independent of the past. Start with step integrands; independent Brownian Gaussian increments give their joint characteristic function. Approximate deterministic continuous g in L2 by step integrands. Itô isometry gives L2 convergence; |exp(iu·z)−exp(iu·w)|<=|u||z−w| gives characteristic-function convergence. The same joint calculation with an arbitrary bounded past measurable variable preserves independence. Uniqueness of finite characteristic functions identifies the Gaussian law; if the library characteristic-function uniqueness theorem cannot be used with its exact finite-law hypotheses, prove this finite Gaussian-convolution specialization locally via Fourier inversion for the smooth Gaussian density. No martingale representation theorem is needed.
2. `def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density`: let phi_v(z)=(2 pi v)^(−d/2)exp(−|z|^2/(2v)); for t>0 define p_t(x)=integral phi_v(t)(x−z) mu(dz), and q(s,x;t,y)=phi_(v(t)−v(s))(y−x). Positive Gaussian integration gives a strictly positive normalized density by Tonelli and the published multivariate-normal density/change-of-variables construction. Its transition law follows from item 1; finite Gaussian covariance addition gives Chapman–Kolmogorov. This definition discharges density existence for this branch, with no assumption that mu itself has a density.
3. `thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation`: on every [epsilon,T], p is C1 in time and C-infinity in space and solves partial_t p=(g(t)^2/2) Delta p. For any finite derivative order, the derivative of phi_v is a polynomial times the same Gaussian; with v bounded below and z in a fixed compact ball, its absolute value on each compact x-neighborhood has a uniform integrable constant. Differentiation under the finite measure integral is therefore justified by dominated convergence. The same calculation differentiates the explicit kernel; integrating its Laplacian gives zero by Gaussian tails. On R^d, uniqueness among probability-law-valued weak forward solutions with narrowly continuous t and prescribed initial law follows by testing against the bounded smooth backward solution h(s,x)=integral phi_(v(t)−v(s))(y−x)f(y)dy for f smooth compactly supported. Cut off h spatially, let the cutoff radius increase using bounded derivatives and finite total mass, then obtain integral f dmu_t=integral h(0,x)mu(dx). Thus the explicit heat semigroup identifies the law; no unspecified boundary condition or uniqueness theorem is invoked. Endpoint h(t)=f is obtained by dominated convergence/Gaussian approximate identity.
4. `thm-gaussian-mixture-score-and-global-lipschitz-bound`: define the posterior weighting nu_(t,x)(dz)=phi_v(t)(x−z)mu(dz)/p_t(x). It is a probability kernel by positive p and measurability. Direct differentiation gives score_t(x)=−[x−m_(t,x)]/v(t), m_(t,x)=integral z nu_(t,x)(dz), and D_x score=−I/v(t)+Cov_nu(Z)/v(t)^2. Since |Z|<=R, ||Cov_nu(Z)||<=R^2. This is a verified global state-Lipschitz/linear-growth contract; it is not asserted for arbitrary unbounded data measures.
5. `def-bayes-reversed-gaussian-smoothing-kernels`: for 0<=u<w<=T−epsilon, define K_(u,w)(y,dx)=p_(T−w)(x)q(T−w,x;T−u,y)dx/p_(T−u)(y), and Y0 law p_T. The forward marginal identity normalizes this probability kernel at every y. Multiplication cancels the intermediate p and forward Chapman–Kolmogorov proves reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov. Iterated Bayes proves its finite-dimensional laws coincide with (X_(T−u)); no abstract infinite product construction is necessary, because the forward process already has continuous paths.
6. `lem-reversed-smoothing-generator-and-martingale`: for compactly supported smooth phi and t=T−u, write the small-time reversed conditional expectation as [P^*_(t−h,t)(p_(t−h)phi)](y)/p_t(y). Differentiate the explicit Gaussian kernel, use the preceding forward equation, and Taylor-expand at h=0 to obtain the generator [L_t^*(p_t phi)−phi L_t^*p_t]/p_t=(g(t)^2/2)Delta phi+g(t)^2 score_t·grad phi. The sign is plus score; the drift of the original pure-noise process is zero. To justify this on compact y neighborhoods, p_t has a strictly positive compact minimum and every differentiated Gaussian convolution is locally uniformly bounded on [epsilon,T]; tails have Gaussian decay since mu is compact. Finite difference quotients thus converge locally uniformly. Differentiate K_(u,w)phi under the integral (or integrate the same generator identity) to get K_(u,w)phi−phi=integral_u^w K_(u,r) Ltilde_r phi dr. Likewise the untouched Wasserstein-gradient-flow and random-matrix prerequisite designs retain their original explicit local obligations; no source reading or proof completion for them is fabricated by this addition.

This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** calibration-proper-losses-and-surrogate-classification / calibration-proper-losses-and-surrogate-classification-examples. **Scope:** For finite labels $Y\\in\\{1,\\ldots,K\\}$, define full reliability by $P(Y\\in\\cdot\\mid g(X))=g(X)$, classwise calibration by $P(Y=y\\mid g_y(X))=g_y(X)$, and top-confidence calibration by $P(Y=\\arg\\max g(X)\\mid\\max g(X))=\\max g(X)$; resolve argmax ties by the smallest class index. For the binary surrogate theorem, take $Y\\in\\{-1,+1\\}$, $\\eta(x)=P(Y=1\\mid X=x)$, convex nondecreasing margin loss $\\Phi$, conditional risk $L_\\Phi(x,u)=\\eta(x)\\Phi(-u)+(1-\\eta(x))\\Phi(u)$, and a measurable extended-real conditional minimizer $h_\\Phi^*(x)\\in\\arg\\min_{u\\in[-\\infty,+\\infty]}L_\\Phi(x,u)$. Define the PC discovery regime locally: a finite set of causally sufficient observed variables, one DAG $G$, a joint law Markov and faithful to $G$, and a perfect conditional-independence oracle for all queried disjoint sets. For distinct vertices $i,k,j$, define the triple $i-k-j$ to be unshielded when $i,j$ are nonadjacent, and a v-structure when its arrows are $i\\to k\\leftarrow j$; a skeleton forgets all edge directions. Define DAG Markov equivalence by equality of the induced d-separation relations, PDAG as a mixed graph with no directed cycle among its already-directed edges, and a consistent DAG extension as an acyclic orientation of all undirected edges that creates no unshielded collider absent from the PDAG. A CPDAG is the unique completed PDAG representing one equivalence class: every directed edge is present with that orientation in every represented DAG, and each undirected edge occurs in both orientations among its consistent extensions. Population PC starts from the complete undirected graph and, at levels $\\ell=0,1,\\ldots$, tests every $\\ell$-element subset of the current neighbors of either endpoint of each adjacent pair in a fixed vertex order; delete $i-j$ on the first oracle result $X_i\\perp X_j\\mid X_S$ and record that $S$. Stop when no adjacent pair has enough neighbors for the next level. Orient an unshielded $i-k-j$ as $i\\to k\\leftarrow j$ when $k\\notin\\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$, then repeatedly apply the background-free Meek rules R1–R3 to closure: R1, $i\\to j-k$ with $i,k$ nonadjacent implies $j\\to k$; R2, $i-j$ with a directed chain $i\\to k\\to j$ implies $i\\to j$; R3, if $i-j$, $i-k$, and $i-\\ell$ are undirected, $k\\to j$ and $\\ell\\to j$, and $k,\\ell$ are nonadjacent, then $i\\to j$. The no-background completion does not use Meek’s separate R4 rule for required/forbidden background orientations.           "statement": "Let $N,d\\ge1$ be positive integers, let $f_i:\\mathbb R^d\\to\\mathbb R$\nbe differentiable, and put $f=N^{-1}\\sum_{i=1}^N f_i$. This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** convolution-and-group-equivariance / convolution-and-group-equivariance-examples. **Scope:** Define discrete convolutional layers with local receptive fields, channel mixing, tied weights, stride and padding; note that common software calls cross-correlation “convolution.” Define group actions $T_g,T'_g$ and equivariance $Φ(T_gx)=T'_gΦ(x)$. For a discrete group $G$, define $[f\\star ψ](g)=∑_{h∈G}f(h)ψ(g^{-1}h)$ when the sum is finite or absolutely convergent, with left action $(L_uf)(g)=f(u^{-1}g)$; the first layer takes $f$ on $ℤ^2$ and outputs on $G$, and later layers take both feature maps and filters on $G$. Cover translation equivariance of standard discrete convolution and Cohen–Welling’s p4 (integer translations and quarter-turns) and p4m (plus reflections) constructions with orientation-indexed features and group convolution across layers. Pointwise nonlinearities commute with the feature-map action; pooling without subsampling preserves equivariance, while subgroup/coset pooling can reduce to subgroup equivariance or invariance. Exact finite-grid equivariance assumes a compatible lattice and boundary convention; cropping, padding, or stride may break symmetry.           "statement": "Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Fix $r>0$ and a nonempty closed convex constraint $D\\subseteq\\Omega$. For every continuous moment path $m:[0,T]\\to\\mathcal H$, the nonautonomous inclusion\n$$\\dot X(t)\\in-\\partial_{\\lambda_V}(V+\\iota_D)(X(t))-d\\Phi_{X(t)}^*\\nabla R(m(t))$$\nhas a unique forward solution from each $X(0)\\in D\\cap Q_r$; its characteristic map is jointly continuous in $(t,X(0))$ and locally Lipschitz in the initial point on each $Q_r$. Let $\\mu_t$ and $\\nu_t$ be two finite-action solutions on $[0,T]$ of the continuity equation with laws concentrated on $D\\cap Q_r$ and velocities\n$$v_t^\\alpha(x)=-\\operatorname{argmin}\\{|q|:q\\in d\\Phi_x^*\\nabla R(m_{\\alpha_t})+\\partial_{\\lambda_V}(V+\\iota_D)(x)\\},\\qquad\\alpha\\in\\{\\mu,\\nu\\},$$\nwhere $m_\\alpha=\\int\\Phi\\,d\\alpha$. The full shifted minimum selection is Borel; it need not be continuous in position. Each finite-action PDE solution with a continuous prescribed feature moment is the pushforward by its unique characteristic map. For starts in $D\\cap Q_r$, these characteristics remain in a larger $Q_R$ uniformly on compact time intervals, and their velocity is the negative full shifted minimum almost everywhere. The same construction applies directly to any continuous forcing $a(t)\\in\\mathcal H$ in place of $\\nabla R(m(t))$. Then for all $t\\in[0,T]$,\n$$W_2(\\mu_t,\\nu_t)\\le e^{(C_r-\\lambda_V)t}W_2(\\mu_0,\\nu_0),\\qquad C_r=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r.$$\nHere $A_r=\\sup_{Q_r}\\|d\\Phi\\|$, $B_r=\\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\\Phi)$, $M_r=\\sup_{Q_r}\\|\\partial V\\|$ in the bounded-selection convention, and $L_r,N_r$ are respectively a Lipschitz constant and a norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\\Phi(Q_r)$. In particular, the localized measure-valued flow is unique for each initial law. The estimate does not assume that $v_t$ is continuous in position.\n\n"

          "statement": "Let $d\\ge1$, let $U\\subset\\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let $f:\\overline U\\to\\mathbb R^d$ be continuous. For $y\\notin f(\\partial U)$, put $K=f^{-1}(\\{y\\})\\cap U$ and define $D(f,U,y)$ by\n\n$$f_*[U]_K=D(f,U,y)[\\mathbb R^d]_{\\{y\\}}\\quad\\text{in }H_d(\\mathbb R^d,\\mathbb R^d\\setminus\\{y\\};\\mathbb Z),$$\n\nwhere $[U]_K$ is the unique relative orientation class restricting to the standard local generator on $K$, and $[\\mathbb R^d]_{\\{y\\}}$ is the positive local generator. This integer is well-defined. It is nonzero only if $f^{-1}(y)\\cap U\\ne\\varnothing$, and $D(\\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$ whenever $y\\in U$. If $U_1,U_2\\subset U$ are disjoint bounded open sets, $y\\notin f(\\partial U_i)$ for $i=1,2$, and every point of $f^{-1}(y)\\cap U$ lies in $U_1\\cup U_2$, then\n\n$$D(f,U,y)=D(f,U_1,y)+D(f,U_2,y).$$\n\nIf $H:[0,1]\\times\\overline U\\to\\mathbb R^d$ and $y:[0,1]\\to\\mathbb R^d$ are continuous and $y(t)\\notin H_t(\\partial U)$ for every $t$, then $D(H_0,U,y(0))=D(H_1,U,y(1))$."

        {
          "id": "lem-mean-field-projection-identities",
          "kind": "lemma",
          "title": "Feature and energy identities for homogeneous projections",
          "deps": [
            "def-feature-measure-energy",
            "def-two-homogeneous-measure-projection",
            "def-partial-one-homogeneous-measure-projection",

          "dependency_level": 2,
          "local_order": 18,
          "justified_by": [],
          "statement": "Let $d\\ge2$, let $\\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $R:\\mathcal H\\to[0,\\infty)$ be continuous, and let $\\Phi:\\mathbb R^d\\to\\mathcal H$ and $V:\\mathbb R^d\\to[0,\\infty)$ be continuous and positively two-homogeneous. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\\lambda$ on $\\mathbb R^d$ with finite second moment, define the feature-measure energy\n$$F(\\lambda):=R\\!\\left(\\int_{\\mathbb R^d}\\Phi(u)d\\lambda(u)\\right)+\\int_{\\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\\lambda(u).$$\nThe integrals are finite because the continuous two-homogeneous maps grow at most quadratically. For every such $\\mu$,\n\n$$\\int_{\\mathbb R^d}\\Phi(u)d\\mu(u)=\\int_{\\mathbb S^{d-1}}\\Phi(\\theta)dh^2(\\mu)(\\theta),\\qquad\\int_{\\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\\mu(u)=\\int_{\\mathbb S^{d-1}}V(\\theta)dh^2(\\mu)(\\theta).$$\n\nIf $(\\mu_n)$ is a sequence of such measures and $h^2(\\mu_n)$ converges weakly as finite measures on the compact sphere to a finite nonnegative measure $\\nu$, then the feature integrals converge in Hilbert norm, the regularizer integrals converge, and $F(\\mu_n)\\to R(\\int_{\\mathbb S^{d-1}}\\Phi d\\nu)+\\int_{\\mathbb S^{d-1}}Vd\\nu$. The continuity of $R$ is the risk premise used for this energy conclusion; it holds in particular under the feature-energy hypotheses.\n\nFor the partially one-homogeneous model, let $\\Theta$ be a closed Euclidean subset, let $\\varphi:\\Theta\\to\\mathcal H$ be bounded and norm-continuous into a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\\widetilde V:\\Theta\\to[0,\\infty)$ be bounded and measurable. Put $\\Phi(w,\\theta)=w\\varphi(\\theta)$ and $V(w,\\theta)=|w|\\widetilde V(\\theta)$. For every finite nonnegative Borel measure $\\mu$ on $\\mathbb R\\times\\Theta$ with $\\int|w|d\\mu<\\infty$ and every $z\\in\\mathcal H$, the exact feature identity is\n$$\\left\\langle z,\\int w\\varphi(\\theta)d\\mu\\right\\rangle=\\int\\langle z,\\varphi(\\theta)\\rangle dh^1(\\mu),$$\nusing the scalar pairing defined in the partial projection, and the penalty inequality is $\\int|w|\\widetilde V(\\theta)d\\mu\\ge\\int\\widetilde Vdh^1(\\mu)$. Define the lifted energy in this model by $F(\\mu)=R(\\int w\\varphi(\\theta)d\\mu)+\\int|w|\\widetilde V(\\theta)d\\mu$. If finite signed projections $h^1(\\mu_n)$ converge narrowly to $\\nu$, meaning convergence against every bounded continuous real test on $\\Theta$, then their feature moments converge weakly in $\\mathcal H$ when $\\varphi$ is bounded and continuous. If AC holds, then for closed Euclidean $\\Theta$ and bounded norm-continuous $\\varphi$ into a separable Hilbert space, they converge in Hilbert norm. Signed projection convergence alone does not imply penalty or full energy convergence for arbitrary lifts."

Fix integers $q\\ge0$, $r\\ge1$, a helper string $s$ independent of $S$, finite nonempty parameter sets $D_1,\\ldots,D_q$ with $|D_j|\\le r$, a nonempty code set $\\mathcal A\\subseteq\\prod_{j=1}^qD_j$ (with the empty product a singleton when $q=0$), a distortion tolerance $\\epsilon>0$, and a confidence level $0<\\delta<1$. For any score map $u$ with measurable coordinates, write $h_u(x)$ for the classifier that chooses the least index attaining the largest coordinate of $u(x)$. For each $a\\in\\mathcal A$, let $g_{s,a}:\\mathcal X\\to\\mathbb R^K$ have measurable coordinates and put $h_{s,a}:=h_{g_{s,a}}$. Equip $\\mathbb R^K$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. For every $z$, assume $g(\\cdot,z)$ is totally differentiable, takes values in $[0,1]$, is $L$-Lipschitz in values, and has a $\\beta$-Lipschitz Euclidean gradient; these mean, respectively,\n\n$$|g(w,z)-g(v,z)|\\le L\\|w-v\\|_2,\\qquad \\|\\nabla_wg(w,z)-\\nabla_wg(v,z)\\|_2\\le\\beta\\|w-v\\|_2$$\n\nfor all $v,w\\in\\mathbb R^d$. No convexity is assumed. Let $S=(Z_1,\\ldots,Z_n)$ be IID with law $P$, and abbreviate $R_P(f_w)=\\int g(w,z)\\,P(dz)$ and $\\widehat R_S(f_w)=n^{-1}\\sum_{i=1}^ng(w,Z_i)$. Then the randomized procedure has uniform replacement stability and absolute expected population-minus-empirical risk gap at most\n\n$$\\left(1+\\frac1{\\beta c}\\right)\\frac{(2cL^2)^{1/(\\beta c+1)}}{n-1}\\,T^{\\beta c/(\\beta c+1)}.$$\n\nIf $L=0$, the right side is interpreted as $0$.           "statement": "Assume AC and use Lebesgue measure for the latent densities. At the observed value $x=(2,4)$, the evidence is finite and positive and the posterior is $N(8/3,4/9)$. Restrict the encoder family to $q_m(z\\mid x)=N(m,4/9)$ for $m\\in[-1,1]$ and choose $m=0$. This encoder is admissible and its reverse-KL gap, with $D_{\\rm KL}(q\\|\\pi):=\\int q(z)\\log(q(z)/\\pi(z))\\,dz$, is $D_{\\rm KL}(q_0(\\cdot\\mid x)\\|\\pi(\\cdot\\mid x))=8>0$, so its ELBO is exactly $8$ below the log evidence.\n\nIn a second model, let $Z\\sim N(0,1)$ and use the standard normal density $h(x)=(2\\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ for $p(x\\mid z)=h(x)$, independent of $z$. This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** finite-metric-transport-duality / finite-metric-transport-duality-examples. **Scope:** For a nonempty finite metric space $X=\\{x_1,\\ldots,x_m\\}$ and probability vectors $p,q$, define couplings $\\pi_{ij}\\ge0$ with marginals $p,q$, $W_1(p,q)=\\min_\\pi\\sum_{ij}d_{ij}\\pi_{ij}$, and prove equality with $\\max_{\\operatorname{Lip}(f)\\le1}\\sum_i(p_i-q_i)f_i$. The coupling set is nonempty and compact, so the primal minimum is attained; constants may be quotiented out by $f_1=0$. **Proof route:** Do not cite unspecified LP duality. Let $c_*$ be the primal minimum and form the cone generated by $(e_i,e_j,d_{ij})$ for all $i,j$, together with $(0,0,1)$. Prove this finitely generated cone is closed: reduce every nonnegative representation to one with linearly independent active generators by eliminating a coefficient along a dependence; from a convergent sequence, pass to a subsequence with a fixed active subset, whose coefficients then converge because the generators are independent. For each $\\epsilon>0$, $(p,q,c_*-\\epsilon)$ is outside the cone. Apply [[thm-strict-separation-of-a-point-from-a-closed-convex-set]] to obtain $(a,b,g)$ with nonpositive pairing on the cone and positive pairing on that point. The slack generator gives $g\\le0$; feasibility of a coupling rules out $g=0$, hence $g<0$. Normalize $u_i=a_i/(-g)$, $v_j=b_j/(-g)$, obtaining $u_i+v_j\\le d_{ij}$ and $\\sum_i p_i u_i+\\sum_jq_jv_j>c_*-\\epsilon$. Set $f_i=\\min_j(d_{ij}-v_j)$; the triangle inequality makes $f$ 1-Lipschitz, while $u_i\\le f_i$ and $-f_j\\ge v_j$, so its single-potential objective is at least the two-potential value. Normalize $f_1=0$; the finite normalized Lipschitz set is compact, so a maximizer exists. Let $\\epsilon\\downarrow0$ and combine with weak duality. Complementary slackness follows by summing the nonnegative primal/dual residuals at an attaining pair. **Examples:** two-point space, finite chain metric, and an attaining primal plan/dual potential pair. **Requires:** finite-dimensional Euclidean separation ([[thm-strict-separation-of-a-point-from-a-closed-convex-set]]) and metric/probability definitions; the closed-cone and transport argument above is a local proof design, not a library theorem. **Sources:** This is the first step of the proposed proof for compact Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality.           "statement": "Assume AC. Fix $t_0<T$, integers $d,r\\ge1$, and a filtered probability space $(\\Omega,\\mathcal F,(\\mathcal F_t)_{t_0\\le t\\le T},P)$ satisfying the usual conditions. Let\n$$dX_t=b(X_t,t)\\,dt+\\sigma(X_t,t)\\,dW_t,\\qquad X_t\\in\\mathbb R^d,$$\nfor $t\\in[t_0,T]$. Assume the drift and diffusion path integrals satisfy $\\int_{t_0}^T|b(X_s,s)|ds<\\infty$ and $\\int_{t_0}^T\\|\\sigma(X_s,s)\\|_F^2ds<\\infty$ almost surely, and that this SDE has a unique nonexplosive strong solution. Put $a=\\sigma\\sigma^{\\mathsf T}$. Also assume the strong restart property: for each deterministic $s\\in[t_0,T]$, the future path $(X_r)_{s\\le r\\le T}$ is almost surely a measurable function of $X_s$ and $(W_r-W_s)_{s\\le r\\le T}$. Assume the coefficients and densities are smooth enough for the displayed derivatives and Itô identities to hold. Assume the marginal density $p_t(x)$ is positive wherever used and is a unique smooth solution of\n$$\\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t,\\qquad L_t^*r=-\\sum_i\\partial_i(b_i r)+\\tfrac12\\sum_{i,j}\\partial_i\\partial_j(a_{ij}r).$$\nDefine the $r$-vector process $\\widetilde W$ by $\\widetilde W_{t_0}=0$ and\n$$d\\widetilde W_t^k=dW_t^k+c_k(X_t,t)\\,dt,\\qquad c_k(x,t)=p_t(x)^{-1}\\sum_i\\partial_i\\!\\left(p_t(x)\\sigma_{ik}(x,t)\\right).$$\nAssume the augmented process $(X,\\widetilde W)$ has a unique smooth joint density solving its augmented forward Kolmogorov equation for $t>t_0$, and for every $t>s\\ge t_0$ its conditional joint density given $\\widetilde W_s$ is the unique smooth solution of the corresponding conditional augmented equation; all displayed derivatives and density integrals are valid. Then the following hold.\n\n1. For $t>s\\ge t_0$, $X_t$ is independent of $\\widetilde W_t-\\widetilde W_s$, and this increment has law $N_r(0,(t-s)I_r)$.\n2. This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** online-decision-protocols / online-decision-protocols-examples. **Scope:** Define the protocol as the learner choosing $x_t$ from past history and then receiving feedback about the round-$t$ loss: full information reveals $f_t$ (or the full expert-loss vector), while bandit feedback reveals only the played loss. Distinguish an oblivious adversary that fixes the loss sequence before learner randomization, a non-anticipating adaptive adversary that chooses $f_t$ from past history before $x_t$, a reactive adversary that sees $x_t$, and a stochastic environment with a specified fixed reward law; state guarantee claims against each separately. Define realized regret against fixed $u$ by $\\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u)$ and static regret by minimizing the comparator term over $u\\in K$; expected regret is the expectation over learner/environment randomness. In a stochastic finite-arm model with means $\\mu_i$, define pseudo-regret $\\bar R_T=\\sum_{t=1}^T(\\mu^*-\\mu_{A_t})$ and distinguish it from the realized reward regret; their expectations agree under the conditional-mean model. Define dynamic regret as $\\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u_t)$ and Hazan’s path length $P(u_{1:T})=1+\\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\\|u_t-u_{t+1}\\|$. Define interval regret on $I=[r,s]$ as $\\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(x_t)-\\min_{u\\in K}\\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(u)$ and adaptive regret as its maximum over all contiguous intervals; call an algorithm strongly adaptive only when, for a stated base algorithm $A_0$ and constants $C,p$, every interval $I$ has regret at most $C(\\log(eT))^p$ times the stated regret bound of $A_0$ at horizon $|I|$. These comparator/feedback/adversary conventions are separate; interval adaptation is not anytime statistical validity.           "statement": "Let $d,T\\ge1$ be integers, let $K\\subseteq\\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $D,G\\ge0$ be finite bounds such that $\\|u-v\\|_2\\le D$ for all $u,v\\in K$ and $\\|g_t\\|_2\\le G$ for every round. Supply $x_1\\in K$. On each round, either $f_t$ is differentiable and convex on an open convex neighborhood of $K$ and $g_t=\\nabla f_t(x_t)$, or $f_t:C_t\\to\\mathbb R$ is convex on a convex set $C_t\\supseteq K$ and a vector $g_t\\in\\partial f_t(x_t)$ is supplied with $f_t(u)\\ge f_t(x_t)+\\langle g_t,u-x_t\\rangle$ explicitly required for every $u\\in K$; here $\\partial f_t(x_t)$ is the set of vectors satisfying that supporting inequality for every point of $C_t$. Run projected online gradient descent with $\\eta_t=D/(G\\sqrt t)$ when $D,G>0$, and with the no-op branch $x_{t+1}=x_t$ if $D=0$ or $G=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice only when $D,G>0$. For every realization satisfying these hypotheses and every $u\\in K$,\n$$\\sum_{t=1}^T\\bigl(f_t(x_t)-f_t(u)\\bigr)\\le\\frac32DG\\sqrt T.$$\nIf $D=0$ or $G=0$, this sum is nonpositive. Whenever the finite-horizon loss sum attains a finite minimum on $K$, the static regret, defined as $\\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\\min_{u\\in K}\\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u)$, is therefore at most $\\frac32DG\\sqrt T$."

          "statement": "Input integers $k,n$ with $1\\le k\\le n$, a confidence parameter $\\delta\\in(0,1)$, and access to an $n$-round $k$-armed stochastic bandit. Output the selected arms $A_1,\\ldots,A_n$.\n\n1. Initialize by choosing each arm once: set $A_t=t$ for $t=1,\\ldots,k$, and observe each reward.\n2. For each round $t=k+1,\\ldots,n$, compute $T_i(t-1)=\\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\\mathbf 1_{\\{A_s=i\\}}$ for every arm $i$. If $T_i(t-1)>0$, first set $\\widehat\\mu_i(t-1)=\\bigl(\\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\\mathbf 1_{\\{A_s=i\\}}Y_s\\bigr)/T_i(t-1)$ and then set $U_i(t-1)=\\widehat\\mu_i(t-1)+\\sqrt{2\\log(1/\\delta)/T_i(t-1)}$. If $T_i(t-1)=0$, set $U_i(t-1)=+\\infty$.\n3. Choose the least index $i$ attaining $\\max_{j\\in[k]}U_j(t-1)$ as $A_t$, then observe $Y_t$."

          "statement": "Let a finite Markov decision process have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. A **differentiable stationary policy family** on $U$ is a family of probabilities $\\pi_\\theta(a\\mid s)$, indexed by $\\theta\\in U$, $s\\in S$, and $a\\in A(s)$, such that $\\sum_{a\\in A(s)}\\pi_\\theta(a\\mid s)=1$, each map $\\theta\\mapsto\\pi_\\theta(a\\mid s)$ is totally differentiable, and for each $s$ there is a fixed nonempty support $B(s)\\subseteq A(s)$ with $\\pi_\\theta(a\\mid s)>0$ for every $a\\in B(s)$ and $\\theta\\in U$, while $\\pi_\\theta(a\\mid s)=0$ for every $a\\notin B(s)$ and $\\theta\\in U$.           "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Choice to form the infinite trajectory laws. Fix $0\\leq\\gamma<1$. An actionless finite Markov reward process (MRP) here means a nonempty finite state set with a joint probability law for next state and reward at each state. Consider the following two MRPs, each with its stated stationary state-weighting distribution, meaning that one transition leaves the distribution unchanged.\n\nIn MRP 1 the state set is $\\{A,B\\}$, with transitions $A\\to B$ receiving reward $0$ deterministically and $B\\to A$ receiving reward $1$ with probability $1/2$ or $B\\to B$ receiving reward $-1$ with probability $1/2$. Its stationary weighting is $\\mu_1(A)=1/3$, $\\mu_1(B)=2/3$.\n\nIn MRP 2 the state set is $\\{A,B,B'\\}$, with transitions $A\\to B$ and $A\\to B'$ each receiving reward $0$ with probability $1/2$, $B\\to A$ receiving reward $1$ deterministically, and $B'\\to B$ or $B'\\to B'$ each receiving reward $-1$ with probability $1/2$. Its stationary weighting is $\\mu_2(A)=\\mu_2(B)=\\mu_2(B')=1/3$.\n\nIn both processes the observed feature is $\\psi(A)=(1,0)$ and $\\psi(B)=\\psi(B')=(0,1)$, so a parameter $w=(a,b)^\\mathsf T$ assigns values $v_w(A)=a$ and $v_w(B)=v_w(B')=b$. Starting from the stated stationary weighting, the two processes induce the same probability law on the observed feature/reward sequence $((\\psi(S_n),R_{n+1}))_{n\\geq0}$. Their mean square Bellman errors, defined as the stationary-weighted square of the conditional expected one-step TD error, are\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\operatorname{BE}_1(a,b)&=\\frac13(\\gamma b-a)^2+\\frac23\\left(\\frac{\\gamma}{2}(a+b)-b\\right)^2,\\\\ \\operatorname{BE}_2(a,b)&=\\frac13\\left((\\gamma b-a)^2+(1+\\gamma a-b)^2+(-1+(\\gamma-1)b)^2\\right).\\end{aligned}\n$$\nMRP 1 has the unique minimizer $(a,b)=(0,0)$ and minimum $0$. With $D=1+\\gamma+\\gamma^2$, MRP 2 has the unique minimizer $(a,b)=\\left(-\\frac{\\gamma}{D},\\frac{\\gamma}{2D}\\right)$ and minimum $\\frac{(\\gamma+2)^2}{6D}$; also $\\operatorname{BE}_2(0,0)=2/3$. For every $0<\\gamma<1$ the minimizing parameters differ. Thus the Bellman-error objective and, for positive discount, its minimizing parameter are not determined by the observable feature/reward sequence law. An MRP here has no action-dependent policy; it is not an unseen-action offline-MDP policy-impossibility claim."

          "title": "The sample CPO update has a well-defined proposal and finite backtracking search",
          "deps": [
            "alg-constrained-policy-optimization",
            "lem-definite-quadratic-forms-have-a-uniform-sphere-bound",

          ],
          "dependency_level": 7,
          "statement": "Under the inputs and assumptions of the sample-based constrained policy\noptimization update, with finite parameter dimension $d$ and nonnegative\ninteger backtracking budget $L$, the update has a unique mathematical output,\neither `no-step` or an accepted parameter. Its proposals satisfy these properties.\n\nIf its matrix $H$ is symmetric positive definite and its local quadratic\nprogram is feasible, the program has a nonempty compact global-maximizer set\nand a unique lexicographically least global maximizer. This is the proposal\nselected by the update and satisfies every linearized cost constraint and\nthe quadratic trust-region constraint.\n\nIf the program is infeasible with one cost and $u_1\\ne0$, the inverse used\nby the update exists, $a=u_1^TH^{-1}u_1>0$, and its recovery proposal is\n$$ x^*=-\\sqrt{2\\delta/a}\\,H^{-1}u_1. $$\nIt is the unique minimizer of $u_1^Tx$ on $\\{x:x^THx/2\\le\\delta\\}$,\nsatisfies $(x^*)^THx^*/2=\\delta$, and decreases the linearized cost by\n$\\sqrt{2\\delta a}$. It need not make the infeasible cost constraint feasible.\nThe non-positive-definite, zero-recovery-gradient and multiple-cost infeasible\nbranches return `no-step` as specified.\n\nOnce the specified exact subproblem decisions and operations have been\nperformed, backtracking terminates after at most $L+1$ candidate tests.\nIt returns the first passing candidate, which belongs to the parameter\ndomain and satisfies the empirical KL and all empirical cost tests, or\nreturns `no-step` if none passes. These are well-definedness and finite-search\nproperties of the exact mathematical update. They do not bound the cost of\nexact feasibility/optimization operations or certify the true expected costs,\nexact population KL, policy improvement, or convergence of sampled iterates.",

This is prose planning, not proof acceptance.\n\n**Pages:** monotone-risk-calibration-and-deployment-guarantees / monotone-risk-calibration-and-deployment-guarantees-examples. **Scope and interfaces:** `def-finite-nested-decision-family-and-bounded-risk`, `alg-finite-grid-conformal-risk-control`, `thm-finite-grid-conformal-risk-control`, `thm-finite-grid-monotone-envelope-risk-control`, `rem-marginal-risk-control-and-adaptive-reuse`. Let the n+1 random loss vectors (L_i(lambda_j))_j be jointly exchangeable across i, measurable, coordinatewise nonincreasing with values in [0,B], and L_i(lambdaM)<=alpha almost surely. Conditional on an independently trained model the same conditions may be required under an actual regular conditional exchangeable law. Scan j increasingly and return the first j with [sum_(i<=n) L_i(lambda_j)+B]/(n+1)<=alpha; if none, return lambdaM. Output the selected prediction rule and pass/fallback status after at most M tests. Then E L_(n+1)(lambda_hat)<=alpha, with expectation over calibration and test data. The guarantee is not P(risk conditional on the realized calibration set<=alpha)>=1−delta, subgroup coverage, or validity after arbitrary reuse of calibration data.\n\n**Argument:** Let lambda' be the first grid member with sum_(i<=n+1) L_i(lambda)/(n+1)<=alpha; it exists because the maximal member satisfies the endpoint condition. If the calibration scan passes at a member, its true all-n+1 average also passes since L_(n+1)<=B; hence lambda'<=lambda_hat, also on fallback. Monotonicity gives L_(n+1)(lambda_hat)<=L_(n+1)(lambda'). The latter selector is symmetric in all n+1 vectors. Exchangeability therefore makes E L_(n+1)(lambda') equal to E of their average at lambda', which is <=alpha. This finite proof needs no selection theorem, right-continuity, or conditional law given a random multiset. For nonmonotone finite losses define the tail-maximum envelope Ltilde_i(lambda_j)=max_(k>=j)L_i(lambda_k); applying the same algorithm to these monotone exchangeable finite vectors bounds the original test loss by pointwise domination, provided their maximal endpoint obeys the safe bound. The price can be conservative predictions.\n\n**Prerequisites:** published exchangeability and finite measurable-selection/rank interfaces from mathematical statistics; ML-64 for the distinction from conformal miscoverage. **Sources:** Angelopoulos et al., Conformal Risk Control arXiv:2208.02814v4 (13 June 2025), entire 19-page extracted text read.
